summary: This standards-track document defines BGP protocol extensions to synchronize flow label states between provider edges for BGP-signaled pseudowires. It applies equally to point-to-point Layer 2 VPNs and updates RFC 4761.

eli5.summary: Two ends of a tunnel must agree whether to put extra tags on packets so traffic can spread nicely. This is how they agree in BGP.

subtitle: Two bits in a BGP attribute let pseudowire endpoints agree on adding a flow label for load balancing.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire normally follows one network path, so it cannot use equal-cost paths for load balancing. RFC 6391 adds a flow label to fix this, but BGP-signaled pseudowires had no way to agree on using it.
tldr.mechanism: The Control Flags field of the Layer2 Info Extended Community gets two new bits: T (the PE will send a flow label) and R (the PE can receive one). A flow label is used only when the sender has T=1 and the receiver has R=1.
tldr.outcome: BGP-signaled pseudowires can opt in to flow-aware load balancing, and older PEs stay compatible because they never set these bits. The document updates RFC 4761.

today: RFC 8395 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4761, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: One Path for a Pseudowire
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries a Layer 2 service across a packet network between two provider edge (PE) routers. By default it is sent over a single network path, even when equal-cost multipath (ECMP) routes exist. That preserves packet order and the characteristics of the emulated service.

This document introduces an optional mode in which a PW can be spread over ECMPs, for example when that is known to help. It builds on the principles of RFC 6391 and augments the BGP signaling of RFC 4761 and RFC 6624. Using a single path remains the default.
sections.eli5: Normally all the cars of one convoy must take the same road so they arrive in order. This RFC lets them split up onto several roads if both ends agree.

sections.title: Flow Labels and Load Balancing
sections.content:
RFC 6391 adds an extra Label Stack Entry, the flow label, at the bottom of the MPLS label stack, right after the PW label. Routers commonly hash the label stack to spread flows over ECMPs, and a flow label tied to a flow chosen by the ingress PE gives the most entropy.

High-bandwidth Ethernet services are a prime example of where this helps. In general, load balancing applies when the attachment circuit bandwidth and the core link bandwidth are of the same order of magnitude. RFC 6391 only defined how to synchronize flow label state using LDP; this document does the same for BGP.

In inter-AS setups, the flow label is never handled by the ASBRs. Only the terminating PEs in each AS push or pop it, so it stays untouched across AS boundaries.
sections.eli5: A sticker on each package tells the sorting machines which package belongs to which group, so they can send groups down different belts evenly.

sections.title: New Control Flags in the Layer2 Info Extended Community
sections.content:
The Layer2 Info Extended Community carries control information for the PWs being set up. Its fields are the extended community type (2 octets), Encaps Type (1 octet), Control Flags (1 octet), Layer-2 MTU (2 octets) and Reserved (2 octets).

The Control Flags byte is a bit vector written ZZZZTRCS. This RFC defines two flags:

  • T: when 1, the PE announces it can send PW packets with a flow label. When 0, it will not.
  • R: when 1, the PE can receive PW packets with a flow label. When 0, it cannot.

C and S are defined in RFC 4761. The remaining Z bits MUST be zero when sending and MUST be ignored when receiving.
sections.eli5: The message the two routers swap has a row of little switches. Two new switches say "I can put on a tag" and "I can read a tag".

sections.title: Signaling the Flow Label
sections.content:
The Layer2 Info Extended Community is advertised in the VPLS BGP NLRI. A PE that wants to send a flow label MUST set T=1 there. A PE willing to receive one MUST set R=1. A PE that receives R=0 MUST NOT include a flow label in the PW packet.

Put together, a flow label is included only when the sender signals T=1 and the receiver signals R=1. With any other combination, a PE MUST NOT include one.

The decision is made per peer. A PE MAY support configuring the T and R bits per service, such as a VPLS VFI, and PEs in one service need not share the same settings. A PE expecting a flow label MAY drop traffic without one, and a PE expecting none MAY drop traffic that has one.

Only the desire to include the flow label is signaled. Its value is a local matter for the ingress PE and is not signaled. Changing the settings may disturb traffic, since the data plane may need reprogramming; that behavior is implementation specific and out of scope.
sections.eli5: A tag is added only when one side says "I will add tags" and the other says "I can read tags". If either says no, no tag is added.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 4761 already says the unspecified Control Flags bits MUST be zero when sending and MUST be ignored when receiving, so the new signaling is backward compatible with existing implementations.

A PE that does not support the extension always advertises R=0, so peers never send it a flow label. It also always advertises T=0, so peers know it will never send one.
sections.eli5: Old routers keep both switches off, so everyone knows not to send them tags. Nothing breaks.

sections.title: The New IANA Registry
sections.content:
RFC 4761 defined the Control Flags bit vector but did not ask for a registry. IANA has now created the "Layer2 Info Extended Community Control Flags Bit Vector" registry.

Its initial contents are T (request to send a flow label) and R (ability to receive a flow label), both from this document, plus C (presence of a Control Word) and S (sequenced delivery of frames) from RFC 4761. The remaining bits are unassigned.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list that says what each switch means, so nobody uses the same switch for two jobs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extension does not change the underlying security issues of BGP-4 (RFC 4271) and RFC 4761. The RFC adds nothing further on the topic.
sections.eli5: The new switches do not make the old risks bigger or smaller.

items.label: Send flow label
items.desc: 1 means the PE announces it can send a PW packet with a flow label.

items.label: Receive flow label
items.desc: 1 means the PE can receive a PW packet with a flow label.

items.label: Must be zero
items.desc: Set to zero on send, ignored on receipt.
